$comment: Written by tools/buildSeason2.ts from tools/season2/design.ts; do not hand-edit.

families.focus: Flick sideways and stop dead; every target sits on one level.
families.why: Horizontal flicks isolated. Wide Wall and 1w3ts mix both axes, so a player who over-travels sideways and one who under-travels vertically get the same score and no hint which they are.

families.focus: Flick up and down; the sideways movement is only ever a correction.
families.why: Vertical flicks isolated. Of the 58 static clicking scenarios measured with 10,000 or more players, 51 spawn targets over a field wider than it is tall (data/season-2/science.json), so vertical stopping gets the least practice.

families.focus: Small moves, smaller targets; settle the crosshair before you click.
families.why: Micro-correction at close spacing, the skill behind 1w2ts and Raw Mouse Control; RawMouseControlClicking3 is replayed 51.6 times per player (data/fun_audit.json).

families.focus: Big flicks across the room; commit to the distance and stop on the target.
families.why: Large-amplitude flicks, which small-field scenarios never ask for. Targets are larger to keep the index of difficulty in the same range as the rest of the category.

families.focus: Five targets up at once; keep a rhythm and take the nearest one next.
families.why: The tempo of 1wall 6targets small and Tile Frenzy (1.29 million and 0.74 million players, data/fun_audit.json), on a field where every target is the same distance away.

families.focus: Targets at two distances; read the size before you decide how far to move.
families.why: Depth. The far ring is half the angular size of the near one, so the same flick distance asks for two different stopping precisions within one run.

families.focus: Slow floaters; match their drift for a moment, then click.
families.why: The entry to moving targets: slow, long-lived paths that reward confirming the shot rather than guessing it. Floating Heads Timing 400% has the most players of any dynamic-clicking scenario in data/fun_audit.json (352,281).

families.focus: Side-to-side swings; click on the swing, not only at the turn.
families.why: Pasu's long horizontal strafes with a predictable reversal, kept on one height so the skill is horizontal timing alone.

families.focus: Read the arc; the top of the bounce is the slowest moment.
families.why: Gravity arcs. A bot under gravity is the one design feature that goes with both more replay and more reach (Spearman +0.10 and +0.13 over 614 catalogued scenarios): small, but the only positive signal on both.

families.focus: Short, erratic twitches; stay with the target instead of chasing its last position.
families.why: Reactive micro-clicking: short strafes at low speed, so the target never travels far but never holds still either.

exceeds.why: Twitching is the idea: reversals faster than any clicking scenario with 20,000 players. It is not new ground - cA 5ts vibrate (11,339 players) reverses every 0.14 s at 1.9 degrees a second and Microshot Avasive (18,028) every 0.68 s at 3.8 - and Jitter moves a little faster than either, from 7.5 degrees a second at Novice.

families.focus: Fast crossers; move with the target and click inside the motion.
families.why: High-speed dynamic clicks. Speed is the other axis of difficulty besides size: at the board median the fitted model prices a doubling of angular speed, 20 to 40 degrees a second, at about 0.8 bits of Fitts difficulty.

families.focus: Three hits to kill; keep matching the movement between clicks.
families.why: Multi-click confirmation on a moving target, which one-hit scenarios never ask for: a miss on the second click is a lost rhythm, not a lost target.

families.focus: Long, smooth strafes; ease into each turn with the target.
families.why: Smoothness on the ground. The target accelerates over a third of a second, so its reversals are gentle and following them cleanly is the whole skill.

families.focus: Mostly up and down; keep the crosshair level with it through each turn.
families.why: Vertical smoothness, which ground tracking barely tests. The target flies, turns vertically about as often as it strafes, and strafes slowly.

families.focus: Curves in both directions; follow the path, do not cut its corners.
families.why: Two-axis smooth tracking: horizontal and vertical reversals on similar clocks draw curves rather than lines.

families.focus: A small, slow target; precision over speed.
families.why: Fine control: at this size the tolerance for drift is under a degree, and at this speed there is no excuse for it.

families.focus: Long jumps under low gravity; carry the crosshair along the arc.
families.why: Smooth diagonal tracking: slow strafes combined with floaty jumps, so the path is an arc rather than a line or a zig-zag.

families.focus: A close target sweeping wide; track with your arm, not only your wrist.
families.why: Close range means large angular speed at a modest real speed: the arm-tracking demand Smoothbot and Close Long Strafes are played for.

families.focus: Close, snappy strafes; react to the turn, do not predict it.
families.why: The close-range strafe duel of Close Fast Strafes (117,749 players, 22.4 plays each, data/fun_audit.json).

families.focus: Strafes and range changes; the target shrinks and grows as it moves.
families.why: Mid-range reactive tracking with forward and back movement, so size and speed change under the player during a strafe.

families.focus: It stops before it turns; stop with it.
families.why: Stop-start movement: a pause before each reversal punishes the player who keeps moving on momentum, a common reactive-tracking fault.
learnsFrom: Flicker Plaza rAim Easy Less Blinks

families.focus: Jumps and short strafes together; follow it up as well as across.
families.why: Reactive tracking through the air, the pattern of Air Angelic 4, which nine of evxl's listed benchmarks use.

families.focus: A flier changing direction on both axes; react on whichever one moves.
families.why: Three-dimensional reactive tracking: short horizontal and vertical reversals on independent clocks.

families.focus: Being tracked makes it turn; stay on it through the dodge.
families.why: Reactive dodging: the target reverses shortly after it is hit, so the longer a player holds on, the more it tests the recovery rather than the lock.

families.focus: Kill, then move straight to the next; no pause between targets.
families.why: The core speed-switching loop on still targets in a compact field: the time between targets is what the score measures.

families.focus: Wide switches; land the flick, then hold.
families.why: Speed switching across a wide field, where the flick between targets is most of the time spent.

families.focus: Switch up and down; stop on each one before you fire.
families.why: Vertical switching, the axis the rest of the category barely uses.

families.focus: Six small targets packed tight; short, exact moves.
families.why: Precision switching: small targets and small moves, the micro side of speed switching.

families.focus: Slow floaters; the switch is the skill, the tracking only has to be clean.
families.why: Speed switching on slow movers, the bridge to evasive switching: EddieTS (185,895 players on its Novice cut) at a gentler pace.

families.focus: Each target takes a while; stay on it to the end, then switch.
families.why: Longer kills on still targets: the discipline of finishing before leaving, which short-kill scenarios never test.

families.focus: Three strafing targets; kill one without losing track of the others.
families.why: The standard evasive-switching problem, targets that move while you are on them and while you are not, at the pace of DriftTS.

families.focus: Targets thrown into the air; catch each one on its arc.
families.why: Airborne switching. Skeet Tracking has the most players of any evasive-switching scenario in data/fun_audit.json (385,771, 31.3 plays each).

families.focus: Fliers changing direction on every axis; pick the next one before this one dies.
families.why: Three-dimensional evasive switching: FlyTS's pattern with vertical reversals on their own clock.

families.focus: Targets heal when left alone; finish every kill you start.
families.why: Regeneration makes leaving early costly: a half-killed target is back to full a second later. Regen Control and tamTargetSwitch are played for exactly this.

families.focus: Fast targets far apart; big switches onto moving targets.
families.why: Evasive switching with speed and distance together: the largest angular demand in the category.

families.focus: Close targets moving fast across the view; stay with them, then turn to the next.
families.why: Close-range evasive switching, where modest real speeds become large angular speeds and every switch is also a tracking catch-up.
